title: Encountering a threat
subtitle: Fast, coarse, and committed before you know what it is
question: What happens when something frightens you?
teaser: A dark room, a shape you cannot make out, and a reaction that starts before you know what it is.
intro: Being frightened is not a feeling that then causes a reaction. Your body commits first, on incomplete information, because being slow is more expensive than being wrong. The feeling arrives alongside — built partly out of the state your body has already put itself in.

events.title: Baseline vigilance is already raised
events.explanation: In a dark, unfamiliar place you are already running hotter than normal. What happens next starts from there, not from calm.
events.science: Context modulates threat responses before any stimulus occurs. The same shape in daylight in your own hallway would produce much less.

events.title: Sampling the environment
events.explanation: Your eyes are working in low light with poor colour and poor detail. What is arriving is genuinely unclear.

events.title: Something moves
events.explanation: Something moves at the edge of your vision. Very little detail, a lot of urgency.

events.title: The fast, coarse route
events.explanation: A quick, rough route gets there first, carrying almost no detail. It is enough to start a reaction.
events.science: The existence of a fast subcortical route for orienting is well supported. Claims that it performs detailed recognition are contested, and we do not make them here.

events.title: Orienting in parallel
events.explanation: At the same time your head and eyes begin turning toward it, before you have identified anything.

events.title: The body is committed
events.explanation: Your body commits. Heart rate, breathing and hormones all change — on evidence that has not been checked yet.
events.science: The bodily response precedes identification. This is a design decision made by evolution: a false alarm is cheap, a missed threat is not.

events.title: Global arousal rises
events.explanation: Alertness systems fire broadly. Every other process in your brain is now running with different settings.

events.title: Attention is seized
events.explanation: The thing gets pushed to the top of the queue. Looking away from it is now genuinely effortful.

events.title: Vision is amplified
events.explanation: Your visual system gets turned up, specifically on the thing that set this off.

events.title: The body becomes information
events.explanation: Your racing heart gets reported back inward. It is part of why the moment feels the way it does, not just a side effect.
events.science: Interoceptive signals are an input to affective experience, not only an output of it. This is why the feeling can outlast the realisation that there was no threat.

events.title: The slow route catches up
events.explanation: The slower, detailed route finishes. It is a coat on a chair. That information was always coming — it was just slower.

events.title: Context is applied
events.explanation: Where you are, what is plausible here, what happened last time. The situation gets taken into account and sent to calm things down.

events.title: Regulation
events.explanation: The response starts being damped. Not switched off — your body has momentum, and settling takes far longer than starting did.
events.science: Regulation is bidirectional and context-dependent, not prefrontal cortex simply overriding the amygdala. Framing it as an override is one of the most common oversimplifications in popular neuroscience.

events.title: The event is encoded strongly
events.explanation: Being stirred up makes things stick. You will remember this corridor, and the coat, for a long time.
events.science: Emotional arousal is associated with better retention of the central details of an event — and often worse retention of the peripheral ones.

events.title: Settling
events.explanation: You know there is nothing there. Your body takes several more minutes to agree.

causalChain.label: Context raises the baseline
causalChain.detail: Darkness and unfamiliarity have already raised the baseline before anything happens.

causalChain.label: Ambiguous motion is detected
causalChain.detail: Low detail, high urgency. Movement at the edge of vision.

causalChain.label: A fast route reaches evaluation
causalChain.detail: A quick route reaches the relevance check before recognition has finished.

causalChain.label: The body is committed
causalChain.detail: Heart rate, breathing and hormones change on incomplete evidence.

causalChain.label: Bodily state becomes input
causalChain.detail: How your body feels becomes part of how the moment feels.

causalChain.label: The slow route resolves it
causalChain.detail: The detailed route finishes and resolves it: no threat.

causalChain.label: Regulation begins
causalChain.detail: Calming down begins, with far more inertia than starting had.

causalChain.label: Strong encoding
causalChain.detail: Being stirred up tips this event toward being remembered.

science.text: Threat-relevant stimuli produce autonomic and behavioural responses with a latency shorter than that of full cortical recognition.
The amygdala contributes to learning associations between cues and outcomes, and to coordinating bodily and attentional responses to relevant stimuli.
Emotional arousal is associated with stronger retention of the central content of an event.
People with amygdala damage can still report feeling afraid. The structure is not where fear is located.
We separate a 'fast' and a 'slow' route into two clean pathways. Both run continuously and in parallel, and the fast one carries less information than the diagram implies.
The heartbeat indicator in the interface is a visual device representing the modelled autonomic response. It is not reading your heart rate, and no physiological value shown here is a measurement.
Calling the amygdala a 'fear centre' is wrong in both directions: it does much more than fear, and fear involves much more than it. This scenario deliberately shows it as one node in a network.
This scenario describes a transient threat response in a healthy system. It is not a model of anxiety disorders, and nothing here should be read as clinical information.

readouts.label: Response initiation speed
readouts.note: How quickly the reaction starts. Fast, because it does not wait to be sure.

readouts.label: False-alarm tendency
readouts.note: How often the model commits to a reaction that turns out to be nothing.

readouts.label: Regulation effectiveness
readouts.note: How well the situation manages to calm the reaction back down.

readouts.label: Encoding strength
readouts.note: How strongly this gets tied into memory.

outcome.headline: A threat response
outcome.body: Your body was committed to a reaction before the information needed to justify it had even arrived. Then recognition caught up, the situation was taken into account, and calming down began — much more slowly than the reaction had started.
outcome.insight: The system is not trying to be accurate. It is trying to be fast enough, and it accepts false alarms as the price. Part of what fear feels like is a body that has already made up its mind.
